message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe – has a rich set of physical, chemical, and nuclear properties that make it unique among the elements. Below is a concise overview of its key characteristics:

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | Protium (¹H), Deuterium (²H), Tritium (³H) |
| | Natural abundance | 99.98 % ¹H, 0.02 % ²H, trace ³H |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | –72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Physical Properties (at STP)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈1/14 of air) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (−423.17 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (−434.49 °F) |
| | Specific heat capacity (gas) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Diffusion coefficient (air) | ~0.00018 m² s⁻¹ |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C |
| **Chemical Properties** | Bond type | Diatomic (H₂) |
| | Bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive limits 4–75 % (v/v) in air |
| | Oxidation state | +1 (in most compounds) |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a weak acid (hydronium ion) in aqueous solution |
| | Basicity | Very weak base (conjugate base H⁻ is unstable) |
| | Redox behavior | Strong reducing agent (e.g., in metal hydrides) |
| | Hydrogen bonding | Forms strong H‑bond networks in H₂O, NH₃, HF |
| | Polarity | Non‑polar H₂, but highly polarizable due to lone pair on H⁻ |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 1 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.792847 µ_N (protium), 0 (deuterium), 2.978 µ_N (tritium) |
| | Half‑life (tritium) | 12.32 years |
| | Radioactivity | Tritium emits β⁻ radiation (β‑decay to ³He) |
| **Applications & Uses** | Energy carrier | Fuel cell (electrolytic) → H₂ + O₂ → H₂O |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid H₂ + liquid O₂ (LH₂/LOX) |
| | Metallurgy | Reducing agent for metal extraction (e.g., iron from ore) |
| | Chemical synthesis | Hydride source (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄) |
| | Medical imaging | ¹H NMR (MRI) – hydrogen nuclei provide signal |
| | Tracer studies | ²H (deuterium) labeling in metabolic pathways |
| | Fusion research | Deuterium–tritium fusion (D-T) → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV |
| **Safety & Handling** | Explosion risk | High in air (4–75 % H₂) |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic; inhalation can displace oxygen → hypoxia |
| | Storage | Cryogenic tanks (LH₂) or high‑pressure cylinders (compressed gas) |
| | Corrosion | Can embrittle metals (hydrogen embrittlement) |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Hydrogen’s low mass gives it the highest specific energy (energy per unit mass) among fuels, making it attractive for space propulsion and fuel cells.
- **Highly reactive**: The single valence electron makes H₂ very reactive, especially under UV light or in the presence of catalysts.
- **Versatile bonding**: Hydrogen forms covalent bonds with almost all other elements, participates in hydrogen bonding (critical for water’s unique properties), and can act as both an acid (H⁺) and a base (H⁻) in different contexts.
- **Isotopic diversity**: The three stable isotopes allow isotope‑specific applications—from tracing metabolic pathways (²H) to nuclear fusion (²H–³H).
- **Safety considerations**: While non‑toxic, hydrogen’s low density and wide flammability range require careful handling to avoid explosions and oxygen displacement.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
